results.title: Minimal Detectable Difference: Definition and Usage
results.content: # Minimal Detectable Difference. The minimal detectable difference is the smallest difference, or change, that can be statistically detected in a given study. It is dependent on your desired significance level, and has been defined as the smallest difference δ where p (δ) ≤ α. In clinical trials, the minimal detectable difference is the smallest difference between treatments that is medically significant. ## Calculating Minimal Detectable Difference. There are many different formulas for calculating the minimal detectable difference, and which one you want to use will depend on your project. Here, α is the significance level you are going for, β is 1 minus the statistical power, and  zα is the 100(1- α) z-score, the percentile of the standard normal distribution. ## Reasons to Find the Minimal Detectable Difference. The minimal detectable difference is important when planning experiments because it gives you the information you need to decide what equipment to use, how accurately to take measurements, and how frequently to sample.

results.title: A principled approach to setting optimal diagnostic thresholds: where ROC and indifference curves meet - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Review article A principled approach to setting optimal diagnostic thresholds: where ROC and indifference curves meet. A test's optimal diagnostic threshold is the threshold that maximizes expected utility. We contend that a test's likelihood ratio is the canonical decision variable and contrast diagnostic thresholds based on likelihood ratio with two popular rules of thumb for choosing a threshold. The indifference curve is tangent to the ROC curve at the optimal threshold. Two indices commonly used to specify the optimal threshold in medical diagnosis are the Youden index, *J*, which is the longest vertical distance between the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and the chance line (the positive diagonal); and an index *K*, which is the shortest distance between errorless performance (the point (0, 1)) and the ROC curve. Here we revisit these and other indices and show that ROCs based on likelihood-ratio criteria provide a principled approach to setting optimal decision thresholds, which are defined as thresholds that maximize expected utility. We then show how indifference curves in conjunction with ROC curves provide a simple graphical way of identifying the decision threshold that maximizes expected utility. The rule is: choose a cut point for which the likelihood ratio equals the product of the prior odds of the disease and the value ratio for the decision, that is, the product of the prior odds and the importance of sensitivity relative to specificity. When the ROC curve is asymmetrical, *J* still prescribes decision thresholds with likelihood ratios of. Next we introduce indifference curves, developed by Edgeworth [24] in 1881, and show how they can identify an optimal decision threshold. Whereas ROC curves evaluate the accuracy of diagnostic tests, indifference curves show what combinations of their sensitivity and specificity are equally desirable. Together, ROC and indifference curves identify a diagnostic decision threshold that achieves any sensible goal, including the goal of maximizing expected utility. Using indifference curves to maximize expected utility is another method described to choose optimal cut-off score while more individualized interpretation of the test results could be achieved using Bayes’ theorem post-test probability estimates according to Bayes’ theorem (Irwin and Irwin, 2011; Foxcroft et al., 2015).

results.title: Minding the Gaps: How to Calculate Materiality Thresholds in Accounting | Numeric
results.content: Materiality thresholds guide financial reporting, auditing, and management decisions, and their use varies across different scenarios:. The materiality threshold is central to financial reporting and auditing as it ensures that financial statements reflect a company's true financial status. Because an audit of financial statements with every single transaction is neither practical nor efficient, materiality thresholds help businesses to better think about what financial data to report and they streamline financial statements for auditors. In an effort to create efficiencies, materiality thresholds help businesses to better think about what financial data to report and they streamline financial statements for auditors. Understanding and applying the materiality threshold ensures that financial statements are both useful and reliable, guiding stakeholders toward sound economic decisions. By understanding and applying these principles, accountants can set appropriate materiality thresholds, ensuring that financial statements are both accurate and useful. By using these methods, auditors can set materiality thresholds that accurately reflect the company's financial realities.
